elements.text: Fracture of the left engine’s front compressor fan hub
Failure of Delta Air Lines’ fluorescent penetrant inspection process to detect a detectable fatigue crack
Presence of a detectable fatigue crack initiating from an area of altered microstructure created during the drilling process by Volvo
The altered microstructure and fatigue crack went undetected at the time of manufacture
Lack of sufficient redundancy in the in-service inspection program
Flightcrew was properly certified and trained
Airplane was properly certificated and maintained
Visual meteorological conditions prevailed; weather was not a factor
Oil observed preflight came from the No. 1 bearing housing and was not a precursor to the accident
Drill breakage or breakdown, combined with localized loss of coolant and chip packing, occurred during drilling, creating altered microstructure and ladder cracking
Fatigue cracks initiated from ladder cracking and began propagating almost immediately after the hub was put into service
Volvo did not identify the altered microstructure as rejectable because it did not match existing inspection templates
Additional templates may assist in detecting potential defects, but additional rejectable conditions may exist
Drilling damage extended much deeper into hole sidewall material than previously anticipated
The crack was large enough to have been detectable during the last fluorescent penetrant inspection at Delta
Significant questions exist about the reliability of flash drying in removing water from cracks
Better techniques are needed to ensure coverage of dry developer powder along hole walls
Absence of a system that formally tracks the timing of part movement through the fluorescent penetrant inspection process was a significant deficiency
Fluorescent penetrant inspection indications remain vulnerable to manual handling and fixture obstruction
Procedural deficiencies in cleaning, drying, processing, and handling might have reduced the effectiveness of the inspection process
Potential deficiencies in Delta’s process may exist at other facilities and contributed to failure to detect cracks in other failed engines
No personal or physical factors would have prevented the FPI inspector from detecting a visible crack
Inadvertent failure of the inspector to systematically search and complete followup diagnosis might have caused the inspector to overlook the crack
Low expectation of finding a crack in a -219 series fan hub might have caused the inspector to overlook or minimize the significance of an indication
Inspector performance may be affected by inspection duration and rest periods, but this has not been adequately studied
Testing methods evaluating inspector capabilities are necessary due to catastrophic consequences of missed cracks
Delta’s nondetection of the crack was caused by failure of cleaning/processing, inspector failure to detect, or a combination
Manufacturing and in-service inspection processes do not provide sufficient redundancy to guarantee defect-free critical rotating titanium parts
Critical rotating titanium engine components are susceptible to manufacturing flaws and resulting cracking
Preflight findings of oil and missing rivets were not factors in the subsequent engine failure
Lack of clarity in written guidance on maintenance discrepancies and irregularities
Captain shut down engines in a timely manner
Evacuation decisions by flight attendants and captain were not improper given available information
Recommendation for reliable means to ensure crewmembers are aware of evacuation decisions
Recommendation for cockpit crews to be aware of exit openings during emergencies
Passenger guidance on emergency exits is not sufficiently specific
